title: Robin Hood
wiki_lead:
Robin Hood is a legendary heroic outlaw originally depicted in English folklore and subsequently featured in literature, theatre, and cinema. According to legend, he was a highly skilled archer and swordsman. In some versions of the legend, he is depicted as being of noble birth, and in modern retellings he is sometimes depicted as having fought in the Crusades before returning to England to find his lands taken by the Sheriff of Nottingham. In the oldest known versions, he is instead a member of the yeoman class. He is traditionally depicted dressed in Lincoln green. Today, he is most closely associated with his practice of "robbing the rich to give to the poor".
Through retellings, additions, and variations, a body of familiar characters associated with Robin Hood has been created. These include his lover, Maid Marian; his band of outlaws, the Merry Men; and his chief opponent, the Sheriff of Nottingham. The Sheriff is often depicted as assisting Prince John in usurping the rightful but absent King Richard, to whom Robin Hood remains loyal. Robin Hood became a popular folk figure in the Late Middle Ages, and his partisanship of the common people and opposition to the Sheriff are some of the earliest-recorded features of the legend, whereas his political interests and setting during the Angevin era developed in later centuries.
The earliest known ballads about him date from the 15th century. There have been numerous variations and adaptations of the story since then, and the story continues to be widely adapted in literature, film, and television media today. Robin Hood is considered one of the best-known tales of English folklore. In popular culture, the term "Robin Hood" is often used to describe a heroic outlaw or rebel against tyranny.
The origins and the historical context of the legend have been debated for centuries. There are numerous references to historical figures with similar names that have been proposed as possible evidence of Robin Hood's actual existence, some dating back to the late 13th century. At least eight plausible origins of the story have been mooted by historians and folklorists, including suggestions that "Robin Hood" was a stock alias used by or in reference to bandits generally.

Ballads and tales
The first clear reference to "rhymes of Robin Hood" occurs in the alliterative poem Piers Plowman, thought to have been composed in the 1370s, followed shortly afterwards by a quotation of a later common proverb, "many men speak of Robin Hood and never shot his bow", in Friar Daw's Reply (c. 1402) and a complaint in Dives and Pauper (1405–1410) that people would rather listen to "tales and songs of Robin Hood" than attend Mass. Robin Hood is also mentioned in a Lollard tract dated to the first half of the 15th century (thus possibly predating the other earliest historical mentions) alongside several other folk heroes such as Guy of Warwick, Bevis of Hampton, and Sir Lybeaus.
However, the earliest surviving copies of the narrative ballads themselves date to the second half of the 15th century or the first decade of the 16th century. In these early accounts, Robin Hood's partisanship of the lower classes, his devotion to the Virgin Mary and associated special regard for women, his outstanding skill as an archer, his anti-clericalism, and his particular animosity towards the Sheriff of Nottingham are already clear. They also feature Little John, Much the Miller's Son, and Will Scarlet (as Will "Scarlok" or "Scathelocke"), although not yet Maid Marian or Friar Tuck. The friar has been part of the legend since at least the later 15th century, when he is mentioned in the script of a Robin Hood play.
In modern popular culture, Robin Hood is typically seen as a contemporary and supporter of the late-12th-century King Richard the Lionheart who was driven to outlawry during the misrule of Richard's brother John while Richard was abroad on the Third Crusade. grok_lead: Robin Hood is a legendary English folk hero and outlaw depicted in late medieval ballads as a skilled yeoman archer who inhabited the forests of Sherwood and Barnsdale, leading a band of companions in acts of defiance against corrupt officials such as sheriffs and abbots. The earliest surviving ballads, such as Robin Hood and the Monk (c. 1450) and A Gest of Robyn Hode (printed c. 1492â1510 but of earlier origin), portray him as a chivalrous figure loyal to the rightful kingâoften Richard Iâwhile targeting exploitative authority, emphasizing prowess in archery, swordplay, and woodland survival over outright philanthropy. Though modern retellings popularized the explicit motif of systematically robbing the rich to give to the poor, early tales show Robin aiding specific victims of injustice, like impoverished knights, and sustaining his merry men from spoils taken from the greedy rather than the broadly wealthy, reflecting yeoman resistance to feudal and clerical overreach. The legend's core elements include Robin's recruitment of allies like Little John and Much the Miller's Son through tests of strength and loyalty, his hospitality toward wayfarers who prove trustworthy, and his ultimate betrayal leading to death by treachery, often at the hands of a prioress. No empirical evidence confirms a singular historical Robin Hood; scholars view the figure as a composite drawn from outlaw archetypes and stock aliases like "Hobbehod" used by 13thâ14th-century criminals, embodying popular medieval grievances against forest laws, taxation, and ecclesiastical wealth amid social upheavals. Over centuries, the tales evolved through oral tradition, printed broadsides, and literary adaptations, influencing cultural archetypes of the noble bandit while resisting romanticization unsupported by primary sources.
